title: Shi: Stories in Stone opens at the Davis Museum, tracing a 1,000-year tradition of stone collecting
summary: For at least a thousand years, collectors in China have gathered and studied shi 石, stones prized for capturing, in miniature, the mountains, clouds and other forms of the natural world. This ancient tradition will be explored in Shi: Stories in Stone , an exhibition that opens Sept. 25 at the Davis Museum at Wellesley College and runs through May 30, 2027. The exhibition is free and open to the public Tuesday through Sunday, 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. The shape of 石 shi, the Chinese character meaning "stone" or "rock," mimics a small stone falling from a high cliff. The word “shi” can be associated with three categories of material: rocks, minerals, and fossils that people have collected and studied for centuries. title: Kimbell's Chardin and original frame restored
summary: The Kimbell Art Museum announced that Jean Siméon Chardin’s The Cut Melon (1760) is back on view following conservation treatment of both the painting and its original frame. Chardin is considered one of the greatest painters of still lifes in the history of art, and The Cut Melon one of his most remarkable works. In its original frame, a rarity for Old Master paintings, the masterpiece can now be seen as it appeared when it was first exhibited, at the Paris Salon in 1761. Acquired last year, the painting arrived at the Kimbell after being preserved in distinguished private collections since the eighteenth century. Prior to cleaning, decades of benign neglect and discolored varnish had veiled the work in warm tones. The conservation treatment allowed for the return of Chardin’s cooler tonality, particularly in the depiction of the marble tabletop, the pitcher, and the melon’s rind. Now revealed to its fullest

title: Overbeck Gesellschaft presents Tirdad Hashemi: The Slow Rhythm of Care
summary: They gather, hold one another, resist, bear witness. Bodies occupy the center of Tirdad Hashemi’s paintings. Set within scenes that move between abstract floral landscapes and burning cities, Hashemi’s figures form bodily constellations through which emotional and political narratives unfold. The artist invites viewers into an intimate, interior world in which everyday gestures and encounters carry the potential for self-determination. Executed in acrylic on canvas, Hashemi’s paintings are characterized by visible brushstrokes and fluid transitions of color that lend the works a sense of immediacy. Loosely drawn figures suggest openness and vulnerability, while gestural marks introduce instability and, at times, violence. title: Studio Museum in Harlem announces first-ever publication of its history
summary: This fall, as the Museum celebrates the final months of its inaugural year and prepares for its sixtieth anniversary in 2028, the Studio Museum in Harlem will publish Studio Museum in Harlem: A History , the first book in the institution's lifetime that details its establishment and traces the organization’s evolution from 1968 to today. Bringing together oral histories from the Museum’s founding figures; essays by leading scholars, curators, and artists; and a trove of never-before-seen archival imagery, this dynamic and comprehensive historical record charts the organization’s catalytic role as a champion for artists of African descent and outlines the lasting impact the Museum has had on the art landscape as a whole. title: Galerie Eva Presenhuber presents sixth solo exhibition by Liam Gillick
summary: Galerie Eva Presenhuber is presenting The Case is Altered or Die Sache ist anders, the gallery’s sixth solo exhibition by the British-American artist Liam Gillick. Liam Gillick’s Mirrored Image: A Volvo Bar, first performed at the Kunstverein Munich in 2007, was later presented at the 21er Haus in Vienna and the Bundeskunsthalle Bonn in 2010. This short performance takes place in a bar next to a Volvo factory, where workers gather to boast about their expertise in building cars. A pivotal moment occurs when a curator arrives from the local museum, asking for help. The director is in the middle of a crisis and is trapped inside the building permanently. title: Heritage Auctions launches stamps category, welcomes philatelic leaders
summary: Heritage Auctions announces the launch of its new Stamps category under the leadership of two of the field’s most accomplished professionals: Charles F. Shreve, who joins Heritage as Vice President, Stamps, and Tracy L. Carey, who joins as Consignment Director. The appointments mark both a new chapter for Heritage and a return to one of its earliest ventures outside of Numismatics. In 1980, Heritage Auctions CEO and Co-Chairman Steve Ivy recruited Shreve to Dallas to establish Steve Ivy Philatelic Auctions, an early rare-stamps enterprise built on the modern marketing principles Ivy had successfully applied to rare coins. Carey began her career with the company in 1988 and became a licensed auctioneer two years later. title: Mudam Luxembourg presents first major European survey of postwar Japanese women artists
summary: In autumn 2026, Mudam Luxembourg – Musée d’Art Moderne Grand-Duc Jean presents the first exhibition in Europe dedicated to women artists from Japan, spanning the period from the postwar era to the turn of the twenty-first century. Bringing together works by pioneering figures from several generations, it examines their contributions to the global artistic landscape while offering a fresh perspective on a crucial yet often overlooked chapter in art history, revealing the important continuities between modern and contemporary practices. Focusing on a period of significant social change, Kaihō: Japanese Women Artists after 1945 explores radical modes of artistic expression that emerged in Japan and its global community across Asia, Europe, United States and Brazil. title: National Gallery appoints Virginia Anderson Head of Art of the Americas
summary: The National Gallery of Art announced today that Virginia Anderson will join the museum as the Christiane Ellis Valone Senior Curator of American Art and head of the art of the Americas. She will assume the role in November. Anderson will lead the art of the Americas department, which stewards the National Gallery’s collection of paintings, sculpture, and decorative arts from the Americas. In this role, she will advance the museum’s continued development of a collection of art of the Americas that is reflective of the broad scope of artistic innovation across various media and time periods. Anderson will oversee a permanent collection of paintings, sculptures, and works of decorative art from the 18th century to present day, including the Kaufman Collection, one of the most significant collections of early American furniture and decorative arts ever assembled. summary: An elegant portrait of a lady by Joshua Johnson, one of America’s first established Black painters; a pair of drawings by Théodore Géricault that reveal his ideas for what became an iconic painting of the 19th century, his Raft of the Medusa; a stunning Tamara de Lempicka portrait that until this year remained in the same family, a gift from the artist almost 90 years ago—each of these remarkable works of art, and more, are among the roster of recent acquisitions by the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston. title: Inma Barrero explores ancient memory and maternal form in new ceramics exhibition
summary: Lévy Gorvy Dayan opened Inma Barrero: MOTHERS, the artist’s first exhibition with the gallery. The presentation brings together eight large-scale sculptures, each on view for the first time, that represent a different maternal presence informed by prehistoric, ancient, and modern worlds across global continents. The sculptures come together to create, in Barrero’s words, a “chorus” of mother figures, “bearing witness and answering one another across the room.” The basis of Barrero’s work is the handmade ceramic bead, with hundreds of beads joining to create a single sculpture. The beads take their inspiration from divine and universal sources, from the artist’s memories of her grandmother’s rosary to Greek komboloi (worry beads), and Buddhist prayer beads, which she encountered while living and working in Kyoto. title: Exhibition explores how museums shape the ways culture is preserved, recorded and made visible
summary: The Korean Cultural Centre UK presents The Unclassified (25 September – 30 November 2026), a group exhibition of four leading contemporary Korean and Korean-heritage artists, Meekyoung Shin, Ayoung Kim, siren eun young jung, and Gala Porras-Kim, exploring how museums shape the way we understand, remember, and interpret culture. The exhibition interrogates the limits of the systems and assumptions through which museums produce cultural knowledge, with works that challenge what can be collected, classified and contained. The Unclassified is presented to coincide with the British Museum’s forthcoming exhibition Korea (opening 1 October 2026) which centres on the acclaimed Lee Kun-hee Collection - one of the most significant private collections in Korean cultural history. Unfolding across four key themes, The Unclassified explores the ways in which museums preserve, record, archive and make culture visible. title: The Baltimore Museum of Art appoints new Curator of European Painting & Sculpture
summary: The Baltimore Museum of Art today announced the appointment of Alexandra Letvin as Senior Curator and Department Head of European Painting and Sculpture. Letvin joins the museum from the Princeton University Art Museum, where she currently serves as the Duane Wilder, Class of 1951, Curator of European Art. An accomplished scholar with a Ph.D. and M.A. in art history from the Johns Hopkins University (JHU), Letvin brings extensive experience developing exhibitions, reinstalling galleries, advancing collections, and presenting European art within broader global narratives. A specialist in the art of early modern Spain, Letvin has organized exhibitions and installations spanning the medieval period to 1945. title: Lonnie Mack's 'Number 7' 1958 Flying V leads Heritage's Vintage Guitars & Musical Instruments Auction
summary: There might not be a rock star as inseparable from one particular guitar as Lonnie Mack and “Number 7,” the 1958 Gibson Flying V that was his primary instrument for almost the entirety of his influential yet underappreciated career. It is no exaggeration to say the course of rock ’n’ roll was directed in part by Mack’s signature guitar, “Number 7” — so named, Mack said, because it was the seventh off the assembly line when Gibson introduced the forward-pointing electric guitar with the arrow-shaped body and head. Journalists seldom wrote about or photographed him without including the guitar in the story or picture, and Rolling Stone even included “Number 7” on its 2019 list of “20 Iconic Guitars.” This piece of rock history is the headline lot at Heritage Auctions’ Oct. 15 Vintage Guitars and Musical Instruments Signature® Auction. title: Noir Blanche presents Josef Fischnaller's surreal photographic transformations in Düsseldorf
summary: Photography begins to lose its familiar boundaries in METAMORPHOSE, a new exhibition by Austrian-born, Berlin-based artist Josef Fischnaller that opened at noir blanche Galerie für Fotografie in Düsseldorf on September 18. On view through October 31, 2026, the exhibition introduces a striking new direction in the work of an artist best known for elaborate photographic restagings of Renaissance and Baroque paintings. For years, Fischnaller has constructed richly detailed portraits and still lifes whose theatrical lighting, sumptuous arrangements and carefully positioned figures draw directly on the visual language of old master painting. title: Salomé Chatriot investigates the post-digital body through 3D sculpture, video, and painting
summary: New media technologies not only expand the ways in which we perceive reality; they also bring something uncanny within it to the surface. As both subject and object of these new realities, the human body has become a central concern of post-digital art. Around a century ago, it was photography—the “objective medium”—that Surrealist artists such as Man Ray and Jacques-André Boiffard used to fragment the living body into strange, object-like parts. The female torso, in its digital, biomorphic abstraction, is also the central motif of Salomé Chatriot’s Void is Seductive. In the sculpture Void is Seductive No. 2, the torso appears mounted on the wall like a trophy: larger than life and clad in black leather, defensive and powerful—somewhere between a BDSM bodysuit, a futuristic sculpture and the Winged Victory of Samothrace. title: Robert Szot debuts new paintings and works on paper at Anita Rogers Gallery
summary: Anita Rogers Gallery is presenting Dust Do Shine, a solo exhibition of new paintings and works on paper by Robert Szot. The exhibition, Szot’s fourth solo exhibition with the gallery, will be on view through October 31 at 494 Greenwich Street, Ground Floor, in New York City. Dust Do Shine marks a significant development in Szot’s practice. While his work has long been characterized by complexity, movement, and layers of visual information, the new paintings introduce larger forms, greater restraint, and more defined spatial structures. Together, the works balance intensity with quiet, and bold color with areas of openness and reflection. Across the exhibition, Szot builds his surfaces through layers of color, metal leaf, drawing, and repeated revision. title: Rachel Howard returns to New York with solo exhibition 'Harvest' at 447 Space
summary: Rachel Howard returns to New York for her first exhibition in the city since 2019 with Harvest, a solo presentation of new paintings at 447 Space. Opening September 25, the exhibition explores the act of witnessing, from the automated eye of an unmanned Reaper drone to the muddied infants referencing Rubens’s Massacre of the Innocents. The paintings strip away historical romance, focusing instead on the stark contrast between sterile technology and human tragedy. At a moment defined by drone warfare, surveillance and the harvesting of data, these new works confront the distance between those who watch and those who are watched. title: Sargent's Daughters presents New York solo debut of Richmond-based painter Alexandra McGowan
summary: Sargent’s Daughters presents Fervor, the New York solo debut of Richmond, VA-based painter Alexandra McGowan. Using fluid and improvisational techniques, McGowan creates radiant fields of color on cotton bedsheets rather than canvas. These works express the safety and joy of queer domestic intimacy, which the artist contrasts with experiences of uncertainty and fear. McGowan's approach to abstraction is affective rather than analytical, allowing viewers to immerse themselves in an emotive visual field. Each work begins with white cotton sheets that match those on the artist’s own bed. Stretched like canvas, they deliberately transgress the boundaries between McGowan’s artistic practice and her intimate life. For McGowan, her bed is symbolic of her queerness – both a place of tenderness and a political signifier. The cotton

title: argos centre for audiovisual arts presents What the Land Remembers—Counter-Archives from Iran
summary: In times of repression, recording becomes an act of defiance. At a moment when war is waged over Iran and communication with the country is constantly under threat, the need to preserve history grows more urgent. This exhibition, two years in the making, feels more important now than ever. With institutionalized terror, internet blackouts, bombings and the destruction of archives, every image becomes a lifeline: a witness, a storyteller and a guardian of collective memory. What the Land Remembers shows how moving images can defy official narratives and protect the stories that political powers try to erase. At its heart lies the Parking Video Library, an independent counter-archive founded in Tehran in 2004 by artist and curator Amirali Ghasemi. title: Memphis Art Museum unveils inaugural art program, major new commissions
summary: Memphis Art Museum announced today details about commissioned, site-specific works by artists Jordan Ann Craig, Yunhee Min, Carlos Rosales-Silva, and Eso Tolson, created for the museum’s streetfront facade, mezzanine and theater, and rooftop “art park in the sky” overlooking the Mississippi River. The works will come into dynamic interplay with their architectural and natural surroundings when the museum opens its new Herzog & de Meuron-designed cultural campus on December 6. The commissioned works are part of an extensive inaugural art program anchored by the major exhibition Making Beauty: Hooks Brothers Studio, 1907-1984, the first museum survey of the acclaimed photography studio’s decades-long documentation of Black life in the urban South. title: Jewish Museum presents major exhibition of Jewish ritual art and Christian cathedral treasures
summary: The Jewish Museum presents a major exhibition this fall that brings Jewish and Christian sacred art from medieval to early modern Europe into dialogue, illuminating complex, interconnected histories across more than six centuries. Sacred Splendor: Jewish Ritual Art and Christian Treasures from St. Vitus Cathedral in Prague features Christian reliquaries on loan from St. Vitus Cathedral—the most extensive presentation of this treasury ever exhibited outside Europe—together with Jewish treasures never before shown in the United States. Through a robust presentation of over 160 objects, the exhibition examines shared urban and artistic environments, and the distinct ritual and theological frameworks that shaped sacred art across Central Europe.
